**Narrative**

The most strongly enriched pathway across the differentially-abundant metabolites is **Tryptophan metabolism** (KEGG map00380; FDR = 0.0, fold-enrichment ≈ 625×). Five of the eight input compounds — L-tryptophan (C00078), serotonin (C00780), melatonin (C01598), 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (C00632), and quinolinic acid (C03722) — are annotated members of this pathway, making it the unambiguous biological driver of the observed metabolomic shift.

The strongest driver compounds are the two terminal intermediates of the kynurenine arm: **quinolinic acid** (C03722) and **3-hydroxyanthranilic acid** (C00632). Both are neuroactive downstream products of tryptophan catabolism, and both are confirmed members of Tryptophan metabolism in KEGG and WikiPathways. **L-Tryptophan** (C00078) is the canonical entry point; a directed KEGG reaction path of four hops (L-tryptophan → N-formyl-L-kynurenine → L-kynurenine → 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid) confirms that the substrate sits upstream of 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid along the kynurenine pathway, consistent with a treatment-induced activation of tryptophan catabolism rather than simple accumulation.

The simultaneous elevation of **serotonin** and **melatonin** points to concurrent activation of the indoleamine branch. Melatonin, serotonin, and quinolinic acid are also jointly annotated in the WikiPathways "ADHD and autism (ASD) pathways" entry, hinting at neuropsychiatric-relevant pathway co-regulation. The presence of **4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutaric acid** (a tricarboxylic acid cycle and glyoxylate shunt metabolite) and **O-phosphoethanolamine** (a phospholipid and glycerophospholipid metabolism intermediate) suggests a broader metabolic re-wiring that extends beyond the tryptophan axis, consistent with the high fold-enrichment of the broad "Biochemical pathways: part I" WikiPathways hit.

The convergence of the kynurenine arm toward quinolinic acid — a known NMDA receptor agonist and NAD⁺ biosynthetic precursor — implies that the treatment drives tryptophan flux toward neuroactive and energy-metabolite outputs. In biological terms, this pattern is consistent with inflammation-driven indoleamine catabolism, where elevated quinolinic acid and 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid are hallmarks of immune activation and have been independently linked to oxidative stress and excitotoxicity in neurological disease contexts.

I have literature support for the neuroactive claim. I now have everything needed to revise the narrative — fixing the three unsupported claims, rephrasing to match confirmed pathway names from the enrichment, and adding the required Limitations paragraph.
